entries.meaning: A large and important town where many people live and work. ---
examples: She moved to the city right after college.
Both cities have great public transportation.
The whole city lost power for six hours.

entries.meaning: A place with houses, stores and streets that is smaller than a city. ---
examples: I grew up in a small town in Ohio.
There are two towns between here and the lake.
The whole town shows up for the parade.

entries.meaning: A very small community in the countryside, smaller than a town. ---
examples: Her grandparents still live in the village.
We drove through three tiny villages on the way.
The village has one store and one gas pump.

entries.meaning: The central business area of an American city. ---
examples: Parking downtown costs a fortune.
Portland has one of the most walkable downtowns in the country.
The new stadium brought life back to downtown.
entries.contrast: American. British speakers say 'the city centre' or 'town centre'.

entries.meaning: A residential area outside the center of a city. ---
examples: They bought a house in a quiet suburb.
The suburbs north of Chicago are expensive.
He commutes in from a suburb forty miles away.

entries.meaning: A small part of a town or city where people live. ---
examples: It's a friendly neighborhood with a lot of kids.
Rents are going up in all the downtown neighborhoods.
There isn't a single grocery store in the neighborhood.
entries.contrast: American spelling. British English writes 'neighbourhood'.

entries.meaning: The stretch of a street between two cross streets, or the buildings on it. ---
examples: The pharmacy is two blocks from here.
They live on the same block as my sister.
We walked around the block to cool off.
entries.contrast: Americans measure walking distance in blocks; British English has no everyday equivalent.

entries.meaning: One of the administrative divisions that a large city is split into. ---
examples: Queens is the largest borough by area.
All five boroughs were under a flood warning.
He's lived in the same borough his whole life.
entries.contrast: The 'gh' is silent: it rhymes with 'furrow', not with 'bore'.

entries.meaning: A poor, crowded part of a city where the housing is in bad condition. ---
examples: He grew up in a slum on the edge of the city.
The city cleared the slums in the 1950s.
That slum has been rebuilt into apartments.

entries.meaning: A public road in a town or city, usually with buildings along it. ---
examples: Our street floods every spring.
The streets were empty at four in the morning.
Cross the street at the light, not here.

entries.meaning: A hard surface built for vehicles to travel on between places. ---
examples: The road to the cabin is gravel.
Icy roads closed the schools.
Take the second road on your right.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'rode', the past tense of 'ride'.

entries.meaning: A wide city street, often lined with trees. ---
examples: The parade goes straight down Fifth Avenue.
Most of the avenues here run north to south.
Her office is on a busy avenue near the park.
entries.contrast: American /-nuː/ (A-vuh-noo); British speakers say /-njuː/ (A-vuh-nyoo).

entries.meaning: A broad city street, often with a planted strip down the middle. ---
examples: Palm trees line the whole boulevard.
The city widened two boulevards last summer.
We rented a place off a quiet boulevard.

entries.meaning: A narrow road, or one of the marked strips a road is divided into. ---
examples: Their house is at the end of a dirt lane.
Two lanes are closed for construction.
Get in the left lane before the bridge.

entries.meaning: A narrow passage between or behind buildings. ---
examples: The restaurant puts its trash out in the alley.
Cats live in the alleys behind the shops.
Don't cut through that alley after dark.

entries.meaning: One of the numbered national highways running between US states. ---
examples: We drove the whole way on the interstate.
Two interstates meet just north of the city.
There's a rest stop ten miles up the interstate.

entries.meaning: The raised stone edge between a sidewalk and the road. ---
examples: Leave the trash cans by the curb.
The city repainted all the yellow curbs.
She tripped stepping off the curb.
entries.contrast: American spelling; British English writes 'kerb' for the stone edge.

entries.meaning: A red eight-sided sign telling drivers to come to a full stop. ---
examples: You have to stop completely at a stop sign.
They added stop signs on both corners.
Somebody knocked over the stop sign last night.

entries.meaning: A tall lamp that lights a road at night. ---
examples: The streetlight outside my window flickers all night.
Half the streetlights on our block are burned out.
We waited under a streetlight for the bus.

entries.meaning: The hard surface of a road or parking area. ---
examples: The bike skidded on the wet pavement.
Heat rose off the pavement all afternoon.
Cracked pavement runs the length of the street.
entries.contrast: In the US 'pavement' is the road surface; in Britain it means the sidewalk.

entries.meaning: A hole worn into the surface of a road. ---
examples: I hit a pothole and blew a tire.
The potholes get worse every winter.
The city finally filled the pothole on our corner.

entries.meaning: A sloping surface joining two levels, or a short road on and off a highway. ---
examples: There's a wheelchair ramp at the side entrance.
Both exit ramps were closed for repaving.
He missed the on ramp and had to circle back.

entries.meaning: A short street closed at one end, with a circle for turning around. ---
examples: The kids play street hockey in the cul-de-sac.
Every house on this block backs onto a cul-de-sac.
There are six cul-de-sacs in the new development.
entries.contrast: The everyday plural is 'cul-de-sacs'; the formal 'culs-de-sac' is rare in speech.

entries.meaning: A part of a road marked off for bicycles. ---
examples: Don't park in the bike lane.
The city added bike lanes on three main streets.
The bike lane just ends at the bridge.

entries.meaning: The time of day when the most people are traveling to or from work. ---
examples: Try to leave before rush hour.
The morning and evening rush hours are both brutal.
The subway is packed during rush hour.

entries.meaning: A marked place along a street where a bus picks up passengers. ---
examples: There's a bus stop right in front of the library.
They moved two bus stops down the block.
I waited twenty minutes at the bus stop.

entries.meaning: The pair of metal rails a train runs on. ---
examples: Never walk on the tracks.
A freight train blocked the track for an hour.
The old tracks were torn up and turned into a trail.

entries.meaning: A barrier with revolving arms that lets one person through at a time. ---
examples: Swipe your card at the turnstile.
Half the turnstiles were broken that morning.
A kid squeezed under the turnstile.

entries.meaning: A bridge that carries one road or railroad over another. ---
examples: Take shelter under the overpass.
They're rebuilding two overpasses this summer.
The truck was too tall for the overpass.
entries.contrast: American. British English says 'flyover'.

entries.meaning: A road or walkway that passes under another road or a railroad. ---
examples: The underpass floods after heavy rain.
Both underpasses are poorly lit.
Walk through the underpass and you'll see the station.

entries.meaning: A passage dug underground or through a hill. ---
examples: The tunnel under the harbor takes ten minutes.
Old service tunnels run beneath the campus.
Turn your headlights on in the tunnel.

entries.meaning: An underground pipe that carries away waste water. ---
examples: The sewer backed up after the storm.
Crews are replacing century-old sewers downtown.
That smell is coming from the sewer.
entries.contrast: Pronounced SOO-ur. A 'sewer' meaning a person who sews is SOH-ur — same spelling, different word.

entries.meaning: A covered opening in a street that workers climb down to reach pipes or cables. ---
examples: Steam was pouring out of the manhole.
Somebody stole two manhole covers on our street.
He drove right over an open manhole.

entries.meaning: A short pipe on a sidewalk that firefighters connect their hoses to. ---
examples: You can't park in front of a fire hydrant.
Kids opened the fire hydrants in the heat wave.
The fire hydrant on the corner is painted yellow.

entries.meaning: A cable that carries electricity above or below the ground. ---
examples: A branch came down on the power line.
Power lines run right behind the houses.
Crews worked all night to fix the power line.

entries.meaning: A large facility that generates electricity. ---
examples: The old coal power plant shut down in 2019.
Two power plants supply the whole region.
You can see the power plant smokestacks from the highway.

entries.meaning: A wall built across a river to hold back water. ---
examples: The dam controls flooding downstream.
There are three dams on this river.
They opened the dam after the spring melt.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'damn'.

entries.meaning: A long line of connected pipes carrying oil, gas or water over a distance. ---
examples: The pipeline runs under the whole valley.
Two pipelines were shut down for inspection.
A leak in the pipeline closed the road.

entries.meaning: A building with several levels where cars are parked. ---
examples: I left the car on level four of the parking garage.
There are two parking garages near the arena.
The parking garage charges by the hour.

entries.meaning: A machine on the sidewalk that you pay to park in a street space. ---
examples: Do you have quarters for the parking meter?
The city replaced the old parking meters with card readers.
The parking meter ran out while we were eating.

entries.meaning: A large outdoor board that carries advertising. ---
examples: There's a huge billboard over the freeway.
Billboards line both sides of the highway.
They rented the billboard for a month.

entries.meaning: A tall building with many floors, usually apartments or offices. ---
examples: They live on the top floor of a high-rise.
New high-rises went up all along the river.
The high-rise blocks the sun from our yard.

entries.meaning: A building divided into separate homes for several households. ---
examples: Our apartment building has a laundry room in the basement.
Three new apartment buildings opened on that block.
The apartment building went up in the 1970s.
entries.contrast: American. British English says 'block of flats'.

entries.meaning: A narrow house of two or more floors joined to others in a row. ---
examples: They bought a townhouse near the park.
The townhouses on that street all look alike.
Our townhouse has a tiny back garden.

entries.meaning: A house divided into two separate homes. ---
examples: We rent the upstairs of a duplex.
Half the street is duplexes.
The duplex has one driveway for both units.
entries.contrast: American /duː/, not /djuː/: DOO-pleks, never DYOO-pleks.

entries.meaning: An apartment that is owned rather than rented, in a building of such units. ---
examples: She sold her condominium and moved south.
The tower holds two hundred condominiums.
Every condominium here pays a monthly fee.

entries.meaning: A small house with only one story. ---
examples: They restored a 1920s bungalow.
The whole street is brick bungalows.
The bungalow has a wide front porch.

entries.meaning: A small building put together roughly out of cheap materials. ---
examples: He lived in a one-room shack by the tracks.
A few fishing shacks stand at the end of the pier.
The wind tore the roof off the shack.

entries.meaning: A very simple small building, often with one room. ---
examples: There's a stone hut at the top of the trail.
The park keeps warming huts open all winter.
We slept in a wooden hut by the lake.

entries.meaning: A building where legal cases are heard. ---
examples: The old courthouse faces the town square.
Reporters waited outside the courthouse all morning.
Several county courthouses still have their original clocks.

entries.meaning: A place run by a city or county where people are locked up, usually for short terms. ---
examples: He spent two nights in jail.
The county jail is over capacity.
Both jails are downtown, near the courthouse.

entries.meaning: A large building where people convicted of serious crimes are kept for long terms. ---
examples: He was sent to a federal prison upstate.
The state closed two prisons last year.
The prison sits ten miles outside town.

entries.meaning: A place where you mail letters and packages and buy stamps. ---
examples: I have to stop at the post office before it closes.
Two small post offices in the county shut down.
The line at the post office went out the door.

entries.meaning: A building where fire trucks and firefighters are based. ---
examples: The fire station is at the end of our street.
The city runs eleven fire stations.
Kids can tour the fire station on Saturdays.

entries.meaning: The local building where police officers work. ---
examples: Report it at the police station on Main.
Both police stations are open around the clock.
He waited an hour at the police station.

entries.meaning: A building where plays or movies are shown to an audience. ---
examples: The theater on Broadway seats a thousand people.
Two movie theaters closed during the pandemic.
We got to the theater just before the curtain.
entries.contrast: American spelling 'theater'; British English writes 'theatre'.

entries.meaning: Film as an art form, or a building where films are shown. ---
examples: She studies French cinema at the university.
A few art-house cinemas survive downtown.
Italian cinema of the sixties changed everything.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: Americans usually call the building a 'movie theater'; 'cinema' most often means film as an art.

entries.meaning: A large indoor building with seats around a central floor for sports and concerts. ---
examples: The arena holds eighteen thousand fans.
Two new arenas opened the same year.
The concert sold out the arena in an hour.

entries.meaning: A place open late at night for dancing and drinking. ---
examples: The nightclub doesn't fill up until midnight.
There's a strip of nightclubs along the waterfront.
The nightclub used to be a movie theater.

entries.meaning: A large outdoor place with rides and games for entertainment. ---
examples: We spent the whole day at the amusement park.
Two amusement parks sit within an hour of the city.
The amusement park closes after Labor Day.

entries.meaning: A place that sells goods to the public. ---
examples: The store on the corner is open till midnight.
Three stores on this block went out of business.
I'm running to the store for milk.
entries.contrast: American. Where Americans say 'store', British speakers usually say 'shop'.

entries.meaning: A small store, or a place where things are made or repaired. ---
examples: There's a little coffee shop next door.
Repair shops line the road out of town.
He took the car to a body shop.
entries.contrast: In American English 'shop' often means a workshop; for a place that sells things, 'store' is the usual word.

entries.meaning: A large building holding many stores under one roof. ---
examples: We used to hang out at the mall on weekends.
Half the malls in the state are half empty.
The mall has a food court on the second floor.

entries.meaning: A large self-service store selling food and household goods. ---
examples: The supermarket opens at seven.
Two supermarkets compete on the same corner.
I do all my shopping at that supermarket.

entries.meaning: A store that sells food and everyday household items. ---
examples: There's a grocery store two blocks over.
The nearest grocery stores are all out by the highway.
The grocery store stays open on holidays.

entries.meaning: A small store open long hours selling snacks, drinks and basic goods. ---
examples: I grabbed a coffee at the convenience store.
Convenience stores here are usually attached to gas stations.
The convenience store is the only thing open at 3 a.m.

entries.meaning: A large store selling many kinds of goods in separate sections. ---
examples: She bought the coat at a department store.
The old department stores downtown are gone.
The department store takes up an entire block.

entries.meaning: A shop that makes and sells bread and pastries. ---
examples: The bakery sells out of croissants by nine.
Two Polish bakeries survive in the neighborhood.
You can smell the bakery from the corner.

entries.meaning: A small store selling sandwiches, cold cuts and prepared foods. ---
examples: Grab me a sandwich at the deli.
There are three delis within a block of the office.
The deli opens at six for the breakfast crowd.

entries.meaning: A place where people pay to sit down and eat meals. ---
examples: That restaurant is booked weeks ahead.
New restaurants keep opening on that street.
We ate at a Thai restaurant near the station.

entries.meaning: A small place serving coffee, drinks and light food. ---
examples: We sat in a cafe and watched the rain.
The cafes along the square fill up at lunch.
There's a cafe inside the bookstore.
entries.contrast: American stress falls on the second syllable: ka-FAY.

entries.meaning: A small informal American restaurant serving simple food all day. ---
examples: We stopped at a diner for pancakes.
Old chrome diners still line that stretch of highway.
The diner has been there since 1954.

entries.meaning: A small shop selling fashionable clothes or gifts. ---
examples: She runs a boutique on the main street.
The boutiques here are far too expensive.
The boutique only carries local designers.

entries.meaning: A shop where men get their hair cut. ---
examples: He's been going to the same barbershop for years.
Two barbershops face each other across the street.
The barbershop still has the red-and-white pole.

entries.meaning: A business where people get their hair, nails or skin done. ---
examples: She booked an appointment at the salon.
There are four nail salons on this block.
The salon opened in the space next to the bakery.
entries.contrast: American stress is on the second syllable: suh-LAHN; British English says SAL-on.

entries.meaning: A machine that sells snacks or drinks when you put money in. ---
examples: The vending machine ate my dollar.
There are vending machines on every floor.
Dinner was whatever the vending machine had left.

entries.meaning: A truck fitted out as a kitchen that sells meals on the street. ---
examples: The taco food truck parks here on Fridays.
A dozen food trucks line up outside the office towers.
That food truck has the best coffee downtown.

entries.meaning: A public area of grass and trees in a town for people to relax in. ---
examples: We walk the dog in the park every morning.
The city keeps up over sixty parks.
The park has a pond and a bandstand.

entries.meaning: An open public space in a town, usually surrounded by buildings. ---
examples: The Christmas tree goes up in the town square.
Several squares in this city date to colonial times.
We sat on a bench in the square and ate lunch.

entries.meaning: An open space enclosed by the walls of a building. ---
examples: There's a fountain in the courtyard.
The building is built around two courtyards.
We ate breakfast out in the courtyard.

entries.meaning: The part of a city that borders a river, lake or harbor. ---
examples: The waterfront is full of restaurants now.
Several old industrial waterfronts have been redeveloped.
We rented a place right on the waterfront.

entries.meaning: A structure or place built in memory of people who died. ---
examples: They laid flowers at the memorial.
Two new memorials were built near the river.
The memorial lists every name in stone.

entries.meaning: The top surface of a building, especially one people can go out on. ---
examples: We watched the fireworks from the rooftop.
Solar panels are going up on rooftops all over town.
There's a bar on the rooftop of the hotel.

entries.meaning: The vertical shaft in a building that contains the stairs. ---
examples: The stairwell smells like fresh paint.
Both stairwells were blocked off.
Take the stairwell to the fourth floor.

entries.meaning: A metal stairway on the outside of a building used to get out in a fire. ---
examples: She sat out on the fire escape to cool off.
Old fire escapes zigzag down the brick walls.
The fire escape is rusted through in places.

entries.meaning: An expensive apartment on the top floor of a tall building. ---
examples: The penthouse has a view of the whole harbor.
Both penthouses sold before the building opened.
There's a private elevator to the penthouse.

entries.meaning: A sheet of canvas or metal stretched over a door or window for shade. ---
examples: We stood under the awning until the rain stopped.
Striped awnings run the length of the block.
The wind tore the awning off the storefront.

entries.meaning: A tall upright post that supports part of a building. ---
examples: A stone pillar holds up the corner of the porch.
Six white pillars line the front of the courthouse.
The pillar is cracked at the base.

entries.meaning: The tall pointed top of a tower, especially on a church. ---
examples: You can see the spire from the highway.
The spires of the old churches still define the skyline.
Lightning struck the spire last summer.

entries.meaning: The details of where a building is, used for mail and directions. ---
examples: Text me the address and I'll meet you there.
We've had three addresses in two years.
The package went to my old address.
entries.contrast: The noun is usually stressed on the first syllable (A-dres); the verb 'to address' takes uh-DRES.

entries.meaning: The number that identifies a postal area in the United States. ---
examples: You forgot the zip code on the envelope.
Rents vary a lot between zip codes.
That whole neighborhood shares one zip code.
entries.contrast: American. British English says 'postcode'.

entries.meaning: Buildings for people to live in, considered together. ---
examples: Affordable housing is scarce in this city.
The town approved housing for two hundred families.
Student housing fills up by April.

entries.meaning: Land and the buildings on it, thought of as property to buy and sell. ---
examples: Real estate downtown has gotten expensive.
She works in commercial real estate.
They put their savings into real estate.

entries.meaning: A building and its land as a countable unit, or ownership and possessions in general. ---
examples: They own a property just outside the city.
The company manages forty rental properties.
Damage to public property carries a fine.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: A marked-off piece of land, especially one meant to be built on. ---
examples: They bought an empty lot on the corner.
Three lots on this street are still for sale.
Kids play ball in the vacant lot.

entries.meaning: A piece of ground where something is built or where something happens. ---
examples: Hard hats are required on the construction site.
The city inspected all four building sites.
This is the site of the old train station.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'sight' and 'cite'.

entries.meaning: The outline that a city's tall buildings make against the sky. ---
examples: The skyline looks incredible at night.
Few skylines are as recognizable as this one.
The new tower changed the whole skyline.

entries.meaning: The rules that decide what may be built in each part of a city. ---
examples: Zoning here doesn't allow a second story.
The council voted to change the zoning on that block.
Strict zoning keeps factories out of the neighborhood.

entries.meaning: A very large and busy city, usually the main one of a region. ---
examples: Chicago grew from a trading post into a metropolis.
A handful of metropolises hold most of the country's population.
The metropolis never really goes quiet.

entries.meaning: A town or city with its own local government. ---
examples: The municipality is responsible for trash pickup.
Neighboring municipalities share a water system.
Our municipality raised property taxes this year.

entries.meaning: A district of a city for police or voting purposes, or the station serving it. ---
examples: They took him down to the precinct for questioning.
Turnout was highest in the downtown precincts.
The 19th precinct covers the whole east side.

entries.meaning: A place where two roads or railroad lines meet or divide. ---
examples: Take the exit just before the junction.
Both junctions are being widened this year.
The town grew up around a railroad junction.

entries.meaning: A building where buses or trains are kept, or a small station. ---
examples: The bus leaves from the depot at six.
Two old rail depots have been turned into restaurants.
We waited inside the depot out of the cold.
entries.contrast: American DEE-poh; British speakers say DEP-oh. The 't' is silent either way.

entries.meaning: The tall pole that a street lamp sits on top of. ---
examples: Someone taped a lost-dog flyer to the lamppost.
Bikes were chained to every lamppost on the block.
He leaned against a lamppost and lit a cigarette.

entries.meaning: A wide road built for fast traffic, with limited entrances and exits. ---
examples: The expressway cuts right through the city.
Two expressways meet just south of downtown.
We got off the expressway at the wrong exit.

entries.meaning: A long bridge on arches carrying a road or railroad across a valley. ---
examples: The train crosses a stone viaduct outside town.
Two viaducts were closed for inspection.
Shops have opened in the arches under the viaduct.

entries.meaning: A bank built along a river to stop it from flooding. ---
examples: The levee held through the worst of the storm.
Engineers reinforced the levees after the flood.
We rode our bikes along the top of the levee.

entries.meaning: A large plant where crude oil or sugar is processed. ---
examples: The refinery employs half the town.
Several refineries line the ship channel.
You can smell the refinery when the wind shifts.

entries.meaning: A city row house faced with reddish-brown stone, typical of the eastern US. ---
examples: They rent the garden floor of a brownstone.
Rows of brownstones line both sides of the street.
The brownstone has the original stoop out front.

entries.meaning: An old, crowded apartment building in a poor part of a city. ---
examples: His grandparents arrived and settled in a tenement.
The tenements on that block were torn down in the sixties.
The tenement had one bathroom for four families.

entries.meaning: An area of land split into lots and built up with similar new houses. ---
examples: They bought in a subdivision out past the mall.
New subdivisions keep pushing into the farmland.
Every house in the subdivision has the same floor plan.

entries.meaning: A tall open space inside a building, usually with a glass roof. ---
examples: Trees grow in the hotel's atrium.
Both office towers have six-story atriums.
The atrium fills with light in the afternoon.
entries.contrast: Plural is 'atriums' or, in formal writing, the Latin 'atria'.

entries.meaning: A covered walkway lined with shops, or a hall full of coin-operated games. ---
examples: The shops run the length of a glass-roofed arcade.
There used to be two arcades at the mall.
We spent all our quarters at the arcade.
entries.русский: крытая галерея с магазинами; зал игровых автоматов

entries.meaning: The flight of steps leading up to the front door of a city house. ---
examples: Neighbors sat out on the stoop all evening.
Kids were playing on the stoops up and down the block.
He left the package on the stoop.
entries.contrast: Distinctly American, especially in New York, for the front steps of a row house.

entries.meaning: A window set into a roof to let daylight in. ---
examples: Rain drums on the skylight all night.
They put two skylights in the kitchen.
The skylight leaked during the storm.
entries.русский: световой люк в крыше, мансардное окно

entries.meaning: The boards or panels covering the outside walls of a house. ---
examples: The hail cracked the vinyl siding.
They're replacing the siding on the whole house.
Peeling siding makes the place look abandoned.

entries.meaning: Walls built of stone or brick, or the work of building them. ---
examples: The masonry on the old church needs repointing.
Water got in behind the masonry.
He does masonry for a living.

entries.meaning: A detailed technical drawing showing how a building is to be built. ---
examples: The architect spread the blueprint across the table.
The city keeps blueprints for every building downtown.
That wall isn't on the original blueprint.

entries.meaning: A wide paved path built for walking, usually beside water. ---
examples: We walked the promenade after dinner.
Palm trees line both promenades along the bay.
The promenade is closed to bikes on weekends.

entries.meaning: A small roofed structure with open sides, built in a park or garden. ---
examples: The band plays in the gazebo on summer evenings.
Two white gazebos sit at either end of the park.
They got married under the gazebo.

entries.meaning: A restaurant that specializes in pizza. ---
examples: There's a good pizzeria on the next block.
Three pizzerias compete on the same corner.
The pizzeria delivers until two in the morning.

entries.meaning: A store that lends money in exchange for goods left as security. ---
examples: He sold the guitar to a pawnshop.
Two pawnshops sit across from the bus station.
The pawnshop window is full of old watches.
entries.contrast: The 'w' is silent: PAWN rhymes with 'lawn'.

entries.meaning: A building where people gamble at card tables and machines. ---
examples: The casino stays open around the clock.
Riverboat casinos line that stretch of the Mississippi.
There's a hotel attached to the casino.

entries.meaning: One of the rounded stones used to pave old streets. ---
examples: The cobblestones are slippery when it rains.
A cobblestone worked loose in the middle of the street.
They uncovered the old cobblestones under the asphalt.

entries.meaning: A metal barrier along the edge of a road to stop cars leaving it. ---
examples: The car slid into the guardrail.
New guardrails went up along the mountain road.
The guardrail is the only thing between you and the drop.

entries.meaning: A tall pointed tower on top of a church. ---
examples: The white steeple is visible for miles.
Steeples rise above the trees in every New England town.
Lightning took the top off the steeple.

entries.meaning: A major highway that drivers pay a toll to use. ---
examples: We took the turnpike the whole way.
The northeastern states are full of turnpikes.
There's a service plaza on the turnpike in ten miles.

entries.meaning: A broad landscaped road, often closed to trucks. ---
examples: The parkway follows the river the whole way.
Both parkways are beautiful in October.
Trucks aren't allowed on the parkway.

entries.meaning: A path built for people to walk along, often raised or covered. ---
examples: A covered walkway connects the two buildings.
The walkways are heated so they don't ice over.
Take the walkway over the highway.

entries.meaning: A tall tank on legs that stores a town's water supply. ---
examples: The town's name is painted on the water tower.
You can see two water towers from the highway.
Kids used to climb the water tower on a dare.

entries.meaning: A row of stores sharing one parking lot along a busy road. ---
examples: The dentist's office is in a strip mall.
Strip malls run for miles along that road.
Half the strip mall is empty storefronts.

entries.meaning: An outdoor market where people sell secondhand goods. ---
examples: I found this lamp at a flea market.
Weekend flea markets fill the old fairgrounds.
The flea market runs from dawn until noon.

entries.meaning: A store selling tools, paint and supplies for repairs. ---
examples: Run to the hardware store and get me some screws.
The old hardware stores downtown all closed.
The hardware store cuts keys while you wait.

entries.meaning: A building with long lanes where people play bowling. ---
examples: His birthday party was at the bowling alley.
Both bowling alleys in town shut down.
The bowling alley has a snack bar in back.

entries.meaning: A business that prepares bodies for burial and holds services. ---
examples: The viewing is at the funeral home on Elm Street.
Two funeral homes serve the whole county.
The funeral home has been family-run for generations.

entries.meaning: An area in a mall or airport with several fast-food counters and shared tables. ---
examples: Meet me in the food court at noon.
Every terminal has its own food court.
The food court was packed with teenagers.

entries.meaning: A raised bank of earth or stone built to carry a road or hold back water. ---
examples: The railroad runs along a high embankment.
Grass embankments rise on both sides of the highway.
The car went off the road and down the embankment.

entries.meaning: A main road that traffic passes along in both directions.
examples: Market Street is the city's main thoroughfare.
Both thoroughfares were closed for the parade.
The thoroughfare is jammed every afternoon.
entries.contrast: The 'gh' is silent and the first syllable is THUR-, not THOR-.
